# Hangul Consonants & Vowels

Hangul (한글) was created in 1443 by King Sejong as a featural alphabet — the shape of each consonant mimics the position of the mouth, and vowels are built from a horizontal line (earth), a vertical line (human), and a dot (heaven, now a short stroke). Modern Hangul uses 14 basic consonants (자음) and 10 basic vowels (모음).

## Core Vocabulary

| Hangul | Romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| ㄱ | g/k | velar stop |
| ㄴ | n | dental nasal |
| ㄷ | d/t | dental stop |
| ㄹ | r/l | liquid (r between vowels, l before consonant or at end) |
| ㅁ | m | bilabial nasal |
| ㅂ | b/p | bilabial stop |
| ㅅ | s | sibilant |
| ㅇ | (silent) / ng | null initial; -ng final |
| ㅈ | j | palatal affricate |
| ㅊ | ch | aspirated palatal |
| ㅋ | k | aspirated velar |
| ㅌ | t | aspirated dental |
| ㅍ | p | aspirated bilabial |
| ㅎ | h | glottal |
| ㅏ | a | "ah" |
| ㅑ | ya | "yah" |
| ㅓ | eo | "uh" (open o) |
| ㅕ | yeo | "yuh" |
| ㅗ | o | "oh" |
| ㅛ | yo | "yoh" |
| ㅜ | u | "oo" |
| ㅠ | yu | "yoo" |
| ㅡ | eu | unrounded "uh" (like the e in "taken") |
| ㅣ | i | "ee" |

## Example Sentences

- **나 (na)** — I (informal)
- **너 (neo)** — you (informal)
- **물 (mul)** — water
- **밥 (bap)** — rice / cooked rice / meal
- **하늘 (haneul)** — sky
- **사람 (saram)** — person

## Grammar / Script Notes

The 14 basic consonants split into a clean three-way contrast within each place of articulation: plain (ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅈ), aspirated (ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ, ㅊ), and tense (ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅉ — written as doubles, covered next lesson). English speakers typically perceive plain ㄱ as "g" between vowels but as "k" word-initially — both are correct because Korean has no English-style voicing distinction; voicing is allophonic.

Vowels come in pairs: ㅏ/ㅑ, ㅓ/ㅕ, ㅗ/ㅛ, ㅜ/ㅠ — adding a stroke turns the vowel into its y-glide version. ㅡ (eu) is the trickiest for English speakers: tongue mid-back, lips spread (not rounded). ㅓ (eo) is open and unrounded, distinct from ㅗ (o).

The letter ㅇ has two jobs: as a syllable-initial it is silent (a placeholder when a syllable starts with a vowel — 아 is just "a"), and as a syllable-final it is the "ng" sound (강 = gang, "river").

## Common Mistakes

- Reading ㅓ as English "o" — it is closer to "uh"; 어 ≠ 오.
- Treating ㄱ at the start of a word as "g" — it is more like an unaspirated "k". 김치 sounds more like "Kimchi" than "Gimchi".
- Confusing ㅡ (eu) with ㅜ (u) — ㅡ has unrounded lips, ㅜ has rounded lips.
- Forgetting that ㅇ is silent at the start: 아 reads "a", not "nga".

## Try It Yourself

1. Write your name using only the consonants and vowels above (ignore tense consonants for now).
2. Read aloud: 나, 너, 물, 밥, 사람, 하늘.
3. Practice the y-glide pairs by alternating: 아-야, 어-여, 오-요, 우-유.
4. Identify the place of articulation (lips / teeth / palate / velum) for each plain stop ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ ㅈ.

## Next Steps

Next we put consonants and vowels together into syllable blocks (글자) and learn how the final consonant slot — batchim (받침) — changes pronunciation.

# Syllable Blocks & Batchim

Korean does not write letters in a linear row like English. Letters cluster into syllable blocks of two, three, or four jamo arranged in a square. Every syllable has an initial (초성), a vowel (중성), and optionally a final consonant called batchim (받침).

## Core Vocabulary

| Hangul | Romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| 가 | ga | block: ㄱ + ㅏ |
| 고 | go | block: ㄱ + ㅗ (vertical stack) |
| 강 | gang | ㄱ + ㅏ + ㅇ (with batchim) |
| 곰 | gom | bear (ㄱ + ㅗ + ㅁ) |
| 책 | chaek | book (ㅊ + ㅐ + ㄱ) |
| 닭 | dak | chicken (with double batchim ㄺ) |
| 값 | gap | price (with double batchim ㅄ) |
| 한국 | hanguk | Korea |
| 학교 | hakgyo | school |
| 사랑 | sarang | love |
| 친구 | chingu | friend |
| 선생님 | seonsaengnim | teacher |
| 안녕 | annyeong | hi / hello |
| 김치 | gimchi | kimchi |
| 서울 | seoul | Seoul |
| 부산 | busan | Busan |
| 산 | san | mountain |
| 강 | gang | river |
| 빵 | ppang | bread |
| 책상 | chaeksang | desk |

## Example Sentences

- **저는 한국 사람입니다.** (Jeoneun hanguk saramimnida.) — I am Korean.
- **이것은 책입니다.** (Igeoseun chaegimnida.) — This is a book.
- **학교에 갑니다.** (Hakgyoe gamnida.) — I go to school.
- **저는 김치를 좋아해요.** (Jeoneun gimchireul joahaeyo.) — I like kimchi.

## Grammar / Script Notes

Block layout depends on the vowel shape. Vertical-line vowels (ㅏ, ㅑ, ㅓ, ㅕ, ㅣ) sit to the right of the initial: 가, 너, 미. Horizontal-line vowels (ㅗ, ㅛ, ㅜ, ㅠ, ㅡ) sit below: 고, 누, 그. Diphthongs combine both directions (ㅘ, ㅙ, ㅝ, ㅞ, ㅢ) and wrap around. The batchim — when present — always sits at the bottom.

There are seven possible batchim *sounds*: ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅇ. Other consonants in the batchim slot collapse to one of these seven by neutralization: 옷 (clothes) is written with ㅅ but pronounced "ot"; 부엌 (kitchen) ends in ㅋ but is pronounced "bueok". This is called 7종성 (seven final-sounds) rule.

Some syllables carry **double batchim** (겹받침) — two consonants stacked side by side at the bottom: ㄳ, ㄵ, ㄶ, ㄺ, ㄻ, ㄼ, ㄽ, ㄾ, ㄿ, ㅀ, ㅄ. Standalone, only one is heard (닭 → "dak", 값 → "gap"); but if a vowel-initial particle follows, the silent half links into the next syllable (값이 → "gap-si", clarifying the ㅅ).

## Common Mistakes

- Writing 가 horizontally as ㄱ ㅏ — Korean blocks must be square; ㄱ goes left, ㅏ right.
- Pronouncing 옷 as "os" — neutralization turns it into "ot" (unreleased t).
- Forgetting that the placeholder ㅇ is silent: 아 is "a" not "nga"; only sentence-final or syllable-final ㅇ is "ng".

## Try It Yourself

1. Stack these jamo into blocks: ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ → ?  ;  ㅁ + ㅜ + ㄹ → ?
2. Read aloud and identify the batchim: 책, 곰, 닭, 사람, 빵.
3. Find the seven possible batchim sounds in this lesson's vocabulary.
4. Write 한국, 서울, 부산 by hand, paying attention to block proportions.

## Next Steps

Next we cover the rules that make written Korean and spoken Korean diverge — assimilation, aspiration, and tensification.

# Pronunciation Rules & Sound Changes

Korean is mostly phonetic, but written and spoken forms diverge in regular ways. Learning the four main sound-change rules — liaison, nasalization, aspiration, and tensification — turns reading from a stutter into fluent speech.

## Core Vocabulary

| Hangul | Romanization (spelling → speech) | English |
|--------|--------------------------------|---------|
| 한국어 | hangugeo (han-gug-eo → han-gu-geo) | Korean language |
| 음악 | eumak (eum-ak → eu-mak) | music |
| 책이에요 | chaegieyo (chaek-i-eyo → chae-gi-e-yo) | it is a book |
| 한국말 | hangungmal (han-guk-mal → han-gung-mal) | Korean (spoken) |
| 식물 | singmul (sik-mul → sing-mul) | plant |
| 입니다 | imnida (ip-ni-da → im-ni-da) | (is/am/are, polite) |
| 좋다 | jota (joh-da → jo-ta) | to be good |
| 좋아요 | joayo | (it is) good |
| 학교 | hakgyo (hak-gyo → hak-kyo) | school |
| 학생 | haksaeng (hak-saeng → hak-ssaeng) | student |
| 갑니다 | gamnida (gap-ni-da → gam-ni-da) | (I) go (formal) |
| 같이 | gachi (gat-i → ga-chi) | together |
| 굳이 | guji (gud-i → gu-ji) | persistently |
| 못해요 | mothaeyo (mot-hae-yo → mo-tae-yo) | cannot do |
| 옷 | ot (written ot, pronounced ot — unreleased) | clothes |
| 옷이 | osi (ot + i → o-si) | clothes (subject) |
| 꽃 | kkot | flower |
| 꽃이 | kkochi (kkot + i → kko-chi) | flower (subject) |
| 백두산 | baekdusan (baek-du-san → baek-tu-san) | Baekdusan mountain |
| 신라 | silla (sin-ra → sil-la) | Silla dynasty |

## Example Sentences

- **이것은 한국어 책이에요.** (Igeoseun hangugeo chaegieyo.) — This is a Korean book.
- **저는 학생입니다.** (Jeoneun haksaengimnida.) — I am a student. ("hak-ssaeng-im-ni-da")
- **음악을 좋아해요.** (Eumageul joahaeyo.) — I like music. ("eu-ma-geul jo-a-hae-yo")
- **같이 갑시다.** (Gachi gapsida.) — Let's go together. ("ga-chi gap-ssi-da")

## Grammar / Script Notes

**Liaison (연음)**: when a syllable ends in a consonant batchim and the next syllable starts with ㅇ (silent), the batchim moves into the next syllable. 음악 is spelled eum-ak but said eu-mak; 책이 (book + subject marker) reads chae-gi, not chaek-i. This is the most common source of beginner confusion.

**Nasalization (비음화)**: stop batchims (ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ) become nasals (ㅇ, ㄴ, ㅁ) before ㄴ or ㅁ. 입니다 is written ip-ni-da but spoken im-ni-da. 한국말 (han-guk-mal) becomes han-gung-mal. 식물 (sik-mul) becomes sing-mul.

**Aspiration (격음화)**: ㅎ combines with neighboring plain stops to form aspirated stops. 좋다 (joh-da) is pronounced jo-ta because ㅎ + ㄷ = ㅌ. 못해요 → mo-tae-yo (ㄷ + ㅎ = ㅌ).

**Tensification (경음화)**: a plain stop after another stop becomes tense. 학교 spelled hak-gyo is heard as hak-kyo; 학생 hak-saeng is heard as hak-ssaeng. The mark of tensification: a "doubled" consonant feel without aspiration.

**Palatalization (구개음화)**: ㄷ or ㅌ + 이 becomes 지 or 치. 같이 spelled gat-i but said ga-chi; 굳이 spelled gud-i but said gu-ji.

## Common Mistakes

- Pronouncing 입니다 letter-by-letter as "ip-ni-da" — natives will hear it as foreign; say "im-ni-da".
- Reading 음악 as "eum-ak" — the ㅁ links forward: "eu-mak".
- Saying 학교 as "hak-gyo" without tensification — "hak-kyo" is the natural pronunciation.
- Forgetting palatalization: 같이 is "gachi", not "gati".

## Try It Yourself

1. Apply liaison: 책 + 이에요 → ? ; 옷 + 을 → ? ; 사람 + 이 → ?
2. Apply nasalization: 십 + 니까 → ? ; 한국 + 말 → ?
3. Read aloud with all rules: 학생입니다, 좋아요, 같이 갑시다.
4. Listen to a Korean song and mark every syllable where the spoken form differs from the spelling.

## Next Steps

With the writing system and pronunciation rules in place, we move into grammar — starting with Korean sentence structure (SOV) and the particle system.

# Sentence Structure & Particles

Korean is a Subject-Object-Verb language: 저는 사과를 먹어요 (I + apple + eat = "I eat an apple"). Word order is flexible because grammatical role is marked by **particles** (조사) attached to nouns. The big four to start with are 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, and 의.

## Core Vocabulary

| Hangul | Romanization | Function |
|--------|--------------|----------|
| 은 / 는 | eun / neun | topic marker (after consonant / vowel) |
| 이 / 가 | i / ga | subject marker (after consonant / vowel) |
| 을 / 를 | eul / reul | object marker (after consonant / vowel) |
| 의 | ui | possessive ("of") |
| 에 | e | location/time ("at, to") |
| 에서 | eseo | action location ("at, from") |
| 와 / 과 | wa / gwa | "and / with" (after vowel / consonant) |
| 도 | do | "also, too" |
| 만 | man | "only" |
| 사과 | sagwa | apple |
| 학교 | hakgyo | school |
| 책 | chaek | book |
| 먹다 | meokda | to eat |
| 가다 | gada | to go |
| 읽다 | ikda | to read |
| 보다 | boda | to see / watch |
| 마시다 | masida | to drink |
| 저 | jeo | I (humble) |
| 나 | na | I (informal) |
| 우리 | uri | we / our |

## Example Sentences

- **저는 학생이에요.** (Jeoneun haksaengieyo.) — I am a student. (topic + predicate)
- **사과가 맛있어요.** (Sagwaga masisseoyo.) — The apple is delicious. (new info subject)
- **저는 사과를 먹어요.** (Jeoneun sagwareul meogeoyo.) — I eat an apple.
- **학교에 가요.** (Hakgyoe gayo.) — I go to school.
- **도서관에서 책을 읽어요.** (Doseogwaneseo chaegeul ilgeoyo.) — I read a book at the library.
- **저의 친구도 한국 사람이에요.** (Jeoui chingudo hanguk saramieyo.) — My friend is also Korean.
- **물만 주세요.** (Mulman juseyo.) — Only water, please.

## Grammar / Script Notes

The hardest beginner contrast is **은/는 vs 이/가**. 은/는 marks the **topic** ("as for X..."); it sets up what the sentence is about and often introduces a contrast. 이/가 marks the **subject**, often the *new* information or the answer to "who/what?". 저는 학생이에요 says "as for me, I'm a student"; 누가 학생이에요? — 제가 학생이에요 ("I am the student") uses 가 because the speaker is the new info.

The shape of each particle depends on whether the preceding noun ends in a consonant or vowel — pick the one that flows: 사람은, 친구는; 책이, 사과가; 책을, 사과를. This is purely euphonic, like English a/an.

**에 vs 에서**: 에 marks a static location or destination (학교에 있어요 = "I'm at school"; 학교에 가요 = "I go to school"). 에서 marks the location *of an action* (학교에서 공부해요 = "I study at school"). Verbs of motion (가다, 오다) take 에; almost everything else takes 에서.

The verb sits at the very end. Negation, tense, honorifics, and politeness all attach to the verb stem after the basic root.

## Common Mistakes

- Always using 은/는 for the subject — say 누가 왔어요? — 제가 왔어요, not *제는 왔어요*.
- Mixing 에 and 에서: *학교에 공부해요 is wrong; use 학교에서 공부해요.
- Forgetting the consonant/vowel rule: *사과은 is wrong; 사과는 (vowel ending → 는).
- Putting the verb mid-sentence: English "I eat apples" ≠ *먹어요 사과를 — Korean must end in the verb.

## Try It Yourself

1. Pick the right particle: 저___ 학생이에요. ; 사과___ 빨개요. ; 책___ 읽어요.
2. Translate using SOV order: "I drink water at the cafe."
3. Replace 은/는 with 이/가 and explain the meaning shift.
4. Make a sentence using 도 ("also") and another with 만 ("only").

## Next Steps

Now that we have nouns + particles + a verb at the end, we need to actually conjugate the verb. Next: the present, past, and future of regular verbs.

# Verb Conjugation Basics

Korean verbs end in -다 in dictionary form: 가다 (to go), 먹다 (to eat), 하다 (to do). To conjugate, drop -다 to get the stem, then add an ending that encodes tense, politeness, and mood. The polite informal -아요/어요/해요 form is the one you'll use most.

## Core Vocabulary

| Hangul | Romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| 가다 | gada | to go |
| 오다 | oda | to come |
| 먹다 | meokda | to eat |
| 마시다 | masida | to drink |
| 보다 | boda | to see / watch |
| 읽다 | ikda | to read |
| 쓰다 | sseuda | to write / use |
| 자다 | jada | to sleep |
| 만들다 | mandeulda | to make |
| 사다 | sada | to buy |
| 팔다 | palda | to sell |
| 듣다 | deutda | to listen (irregular) |
| 살다 | salda | to live |
| 공부하다 | gongbuhada | to study |
| 일하다 | ilhada | to work |
| 좋아하다 | joahada | to like |
| 가요 | gayo | (I) go |
| 먹어요 | meogeoyo | (I) eat |
| 했어요 | haesseoyo | (I) did |
| 갈 거예요 | gal geoyeyo | (I) will go |

## Example Sentences

- **저는 학교에 가요.** (Jeoneun hakgyoe gayo.) — I go to school.
- **저는 김치를 먹어요.** (Jeoneun gimchireul meogeoyo.) — I eat kimchi.
- **친구가 와요.** (Chinguga wayo.) — A friend is coming.
- **어제 영화를 봤어요.** (Eoje yeonghwareul bwasseoyo.) — I watched a movie yesterday.
- **내일 공부할 거예요.** (Naeil gongbuhal geoyeyo.) — I will study tomorrow.
- **한국어를 좋아해요.** (Hangugeoreul joahaeyo.) — I like Korean.

## Grammar / Script Notes

**Present polite (해요체)** — drop -다 from the stem, then add an ending chosen by the last vowel of the stem:
- Stem ends in ㅏ or ㅗ → add -아요: 가다 → 가 + 아요 → 가요 (the same vowel contracts).
- Stem ends in any other vowel → add -어요: 먹다 → 먹어요; 마시다 → 마시 + 어요 → 마셔요.
- Stems ending in 하 → 해요: 공부하다 → 공부해요.

**Past tense** swaps the 요 for 었어요 / 았어요 (matching the same vowel rule), or 했어요 for 하다 verbs. 가다 → 갔어요. 먹다 → 먹었어요. 공부하다 → 공부했어요.

**Future / probability** — attach -(으)ㄹ 거예요 to the stem: 가다 → 갈 거예요 (I will go), 먹다 → 먹을 거예요 (I will eat). The 으 appears after consonant-final stems for ease of pronunciation.

**Vowel contraction** is a constant feature: 가 + 아요 = 가요 (not 가아요), 보 + 아요 = 봐요, 마시 + 어요 = 마셔요, 오 + 아요 = 와요. Memorize the contracted forms — they are how Koreans actually speak.

## Common Mistakes

- Not contracting: *가아요 instead of 가요. The contracted form is the only one used.
- Picking the wrong ending vowel: *먹아요 (should be 먹어요 — last vowel is ㅓ, not ㅏ/ㅗ).
- Treating 듣다 as regular: it is irregular and becomes 들어요 (the ㄷ → ㄹ before vowel endings).
- Forgetting that 하다 is its own pattern: 해요, 했어요, 할 거예요.

## Try It Yourself

1. Conjugate to present polite: 마시다 → ?; 보다 → ?; 읽다 → ?; 쓰다 → ?.
2. Convert to past tense: 가요 → ?; 먹어요 → ?; 공부해요 → ?.
3. Make a future-tense sentence: "I will read this book tomorrow."
4. Pick three verbs and write a daily-routine sentence for each.

## Next Steps

You can conjugate now — but Korean has more than one politeness register. Next we learn the seven speech levels and when to switch between them.

# Honorifics & Speech Levels

Korean grammar encodes who you are speaking *to* (speech level) and who you are speaking *about* (subject honorifics). Beginners need to master 합니다체 (formal polite), 해요체 (informal polite), and 해체 (casual). Advanced speakers add subject honorifics like -(으)시- and special vocabulary for elders.

## Core Vocabulary

| Hangul | Romanization | English / function |
|--------|--------------|-------------------|
| 합니다체 | hamnida-che | formal polite (news, business) |
| 해요체 | haeyo-che | informal polite (everyday) |
| 해체 | hae-che | casual (close friends, family) |
| 하십시오체 | hasipsio-che | most formal (announcements) |
| -(으)시- | -(eu)si- | subject honorific infix |
| 께서 | kkeseo | honorific subject marker (replaces 가/이) |
| 께 | kke | honorific dative (replaces 에게) |
| 잡수시다 | japsusida | to eat (honorific of 먹다) |
| 주무시다 | jumusida | to sleep (honorific of 자다) |
| 계시다 | gyesida | to be / exist (honorific of 있다) |
| 말씀하시다 | malsseumhasida | to speak (honorific of 말하다) |
| 진지 | jinji | meal (honorific of 밥) |
| 댁 | daek | home (honorific of 집) |
| 분 | bun | person (honorific counter for 사람) |
| 선생님 | seonsaengnim | teacher (with respectful -님) |
| 어머님 | eomeonim | mother (respectful) |
| 사장님 | sajangnim | company president |
| 안녕하십니까 | annyeonghasimnikka | hello (formal) |
| 안녕하세요 | annyeonghaseyo | hello (informal polite) |
| 안녕 | annyeong | hi (casual) |

## Example Sentences

- **안녕하십니까. 저는 김민수입니다.** (Annyeonghasimnikka. Jeoneun Gim Minsu-imnida.) — Hello. I am Kim Minsu. (formal)
- **안녕하세요. 저는 김민수예요.** (Annyeonghaseyo. Jeoneun Gim Minsu-yeyo.) — Hello, I'm Kim Minsu. (everyday polite)
- **할아버지께서 진지를 잡수세요.** (Harabeojikkeseo jinjireul japsuseyo.) — Grandfather is eating his meal.
- **선생님께서 학교에 계세요.** (Seonsaengnimkkeseo hakgyoe gyeseyo.) — The teacher is at school.
- **어머니께 선물을 드렸어요.** (Eomeonikke seonmureul deuryeosseoyo.) — I gave a gift to mother.

## Grammar / Script Notes

**Three core levels** for daily life:
- 합니다체 (formal polite): -ㅂ니다 / -습니다. Used in news broadcasts, business meetings, military, formal speeches. 갑니다, 먹습니다, 입니다.
- 해요체 (informal polite): -아요 / -어요 / -해요. The default for adults speaking to people they don't know intimately. 가요, 먹어요, 해요.
- 해체 (casual): -아 / -어 / -해 (just drop the 요). Used among close friends and to younger family. 가, 먹어, 해. Using this with strangers is rude.

**Subject honorifics** (-(으)시-) elevate the *subject* of the verb when that subject deserves respect (older relatives, teachers, bosses). It infixes before the tense ending: 가다 → 가시다 → 가세요 (informal polite) / 가십니다 (formal polite). Some verbs and nouns have entirely different honorific forms: 먹다 → 잡수시다, 자다 → 주무시다, 있다 → 계시다, 집 → 댁.

**Honorific particles** replace the plain ones when the subject is honorable: 이/가 → 께서; 에게 → 께. So "Father is sleeping" is 아버지께서 주무세요, not *아버지가 자요.

The suffix **-님** attaches to titles and (sometimes) names to elevate them: 선생님 (teacher), 사장님 (boss), 어머님 (mother, said by adult speaker).

## Common Mistakes

- Using 해체 (가, 먹어) with strangers — use 해요체 by default until invited otherwise.
- Forgetting that you do *not* use -(으)시- on yourself — *저는 학생이세요 is wrong; 저는 학생이에요.
- Dropping -님 from 선생님 in direct address — always say 선생님, never just 선생.
- Mixing up subject and listener honorifics: 갑니다 (formal *to listener*) ≠ 가십니다 (subject is honored, formal to listener).

## Try It Yourself

1. Convert to all three levels: "I eat" → 합니다 / 해요 / 해체.
2. Write a sentence about your father using -(으)시- and 께서.
3. Greet your boss in 합니다체, your colleague in 해요체, your sibling in 해체.
4. Replace plain verbs with their honorific forms in: 할머니가 집에서 밥을 먹어요.

## Next Steps

Grammar foundations are in place. Now we expand vocabulary — starting with Korea's two parallel number systems.

# Numbers & Counting Systems

Korean has **two complete number systems**: native Korean (하나, 둘, 셋…) and Sino-Korean (일, 이, 삼…). Each is used in different contexts — age and counting things uses native Korean; dates, money, and phone numbers use Sino-Korean. Counters (단위 명사) attach to the number to specify what is being counted.

## Core Vocabulary

| Hangul | Romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| 하나 / 한 | hana / han | one (native; 한 before counters) |
| 둘 / 두 | dul / du | two (native) |
| 셋 / 세 | set / se | three (native) |
| 넷 / 네 | net / ne | four (native) |
| 다섯 | daseot | five (native) |
| 여섯 | yeoseot | six (native) |
| 일곱 | ilgop | seven (native) |
| 여덟 | yeodeol | eight (native) |
| 아홉 | ahop | nine (native) |
| 열 | yeol | ten (native) |
| 스물 / 스무 | seumul / seumu | twenty (native) |
| 일 | il | one (Sino-Korean) |
| 이 | i | two (Sino) |
| 삼 | sam | three (Sino) |
| 사 | sa | four (Sino) |
| 오 | o | five (Sino) |
| 육 | yuk | six (Sino) |
| 칠 | chil | seven (Sino) |
| 팔 | pal | eight (Sino) |
| 구 | gu | nine (Sino) |
| 십 | sip | ten (Sino) |
| 백 | baek | hundred (Sino) |
| 천 | cheon | thousand (Sino) |
| 만 | man | ten thousand (Sino) |
| 명 | myeong | counter for people |
| 개 | gae | counter for objects |
| 살 | sal | counter for age |
| 시 | si | counter for hours (o'clock) |
| 분 | bun | counter for minutes |
| 원 | won | Korean currency |

## Example Sentences

- **사과 두 개 주세요.** (Sagwa du gae juseyo.) — Two apples, please.
- **저는 스물다섯 살이에요.** (Jeoneun seumuldaseot sarieyo.) — I am 25 years old.
- **세 시 삼십 분이에요.** (Se si samsip bunieyo.) — It's 3:30.
- **이천이십육 년이에요.** (Icheon-isip-yuk nyeonieyo.) — It's the year 2026.
- **만 원이에요.** (Man wonieyo.) — It's 10,000 won.
- **친구 다섯 명이 와요.** (Chingu daseot myeongi wayo.) — Five friends are coming.

## Grammar / Script Notes

**Use native Korean** for: counting things (사과 두 개), people (다섯 명), age (스무 살), hours of the clock (세 시 = 3 o'clock). Native Korean only goes up to 99 (아흔아홉); above that, switch to Sino.

**Use Sino-Korean** for: minutes (삼십 분 = 30 minutes), money (만 원), dates (이월 = February), phone numbers, addresses, math, and any number above 99.

The native numbers 하나/둘/셋/넷/스물 shorten to 한/두/세/네/스무 when followed by a counter. So you say 한 명 (one person), not 하나 명. This shortening is mandatory.

**Korean groups by 만 (10,000), not by thousand.** 100,000 is 십만 (ten 10,000s), 1,000,000 is 백만 (hundred 10,000s), and 100,000,000 is 억 (one 100-million). When converting big numbers from English, divide by 10,000 first.

Counters attach without spaces in the number-counter pair but with a space before the noun: 학생 다섯 명 (five students), 책 두 권 (two books, using 권 for books).

## Common Mistakes

- Mixing systems: *오 살 (Sino + age) is wrong; age uses native: 다섯 살.
- Forgetting the shortening: *둘 명 should be 두 명.
- Treating 만 like a "thousand" — 만 is *ten thousand*, so 30,000 is 삼만 (three ten-thousands), not *삼십천.
- Using 개 for people: *학생 다섯 개 is wrong; people use 명, not 개.

## Try It Yourself

1. Say your age in Korean (native) and your phone number (Sino).
2. Tell the time: 7:45, 11:30, 1:15 (use 시 + 분).
3. Count: 3 books (책 + 권), 5 cars (자동차 + 대), 2 cups of coffee (커피 + 잔).
4. Convert to Korean: 35,000 won; 120,000 people; the year 1988.

## Next Steps

Numbers unlock daily transactions. Next we cover the everyday vocabulary fields you'll lean on most: family, food, and daily life.

# Family, Food & Daily Life

Korean family terms encode age and side of the family: an older brother is 형 (to a male) or 오빠 (to a female). Food vocabulary opens the door to ordering and reading menus — Korea's food culture is famous for a reason.

## Core Vocabulary

| Hangul | Romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| 가족 | gajok | family |
| 아버지 / 아빠 | abeoji / appa | father / dad |
| 어머니 / 엄마 | eomeoni / eomma | mother / mom |
| 형 | hyeong | older brother (male speaker) |
| 오빠 | oppa | older brother (female speaker) |
| 누나 | nuna | older sister (male speaker) |
| 언니 | eonni | older sister (female speaker) |
| 동생 | dongsaeng | younger sibling |
| 남동생 / 여동생 | namdongsaeng / yeodongsaeng | younger brother / sister |
| 할아버지 / 할머니 | harabeoji / halmeoni | grandfather / grandmother |
| 아들 / 딸 | adeul / ttal | son / daughter |
| 남편 / 아내 | nampyeon / anae | husband / wife |
| 밥 | bap | rice / meal |
| 김치 | gimchi | kimchi |
| 김밥 | gimbap | seaweed rice rolls |
| 비빔밥 | bibimbap | mixed rice bowl |
| 불고기 | bulgogi | marinated grilled beef |
| 찌개 | jjigae | stew |
| 라면 | ramyeon | ramen |
| 국 | guk | soup |
| 반찬 | banchan | side dishes |
| 물 | mul | water |
| 차 | cha | tea |
| 커피 | keopi | coffee |
| 아침 / 점심 / 저녁 | achim / jeomsim / jeonyeok | breakfast / lunch / dinner |
| 일어나다 | ireonada | to wake up |
| 씻다 | ssitda | to wash |
| 먹다 | meokda | to eat |
| 자다 | jada | to sleep |

## Example Sentences

- **저희 가족은 네 명이에요.** (Jeohui gajogeun ne myeongieyo.) — My family has four people.
- **저는 언니가 한 명 있어요.** (Jeoneun eonniga han myeong isseoyo.) — I (female speaker) have one older sister.
- **아침에 빵을 먹고 커피를 마셔요.** (Achime ppangeul meokgo keopireul masyeoyo.) — In the morning I eat bread and drink coffee.
- **저녁에 김치찌개를 만들었어요.** (Jeonyeoge gimchijjigaereul mandeureosseoyo.) — I made kimchi stew for dinner.
- **할머니께서는 비빔밥을 좋아하세요.** (Halmeonikkeseoneun bibimbabeul joahaseyo.) — Grandmother likes bibimbap.

## Grammar / Script Notes

The kinship system splits sibling terms by the speaker's gender: a male calls his older brother 형, a female calls hers 오빠. Misusing this signals you don't know the system. Younger siblings are gender-neutral 동생, with optional 남/여 prefix to disambiguate.

When talking about your *own* family, use the humble 저희 instead of 우리 in formal settings: 저희 어머니 ("my mother"). For someone else's family, add -님 to elevate: 어머님, 아버님, 형님.

Korean meals always include 반찬 (side dishes) — kimchi is not optional, and most restaurant meals come with 3-6 small dishes free. A typical breakfast/lunch/dinner is built on 밥 (rice) + 국 (soup) + 반찬 + a main protein. Stews end in 찌개 (thicker) or 탕 (clearer): 김치찌개, 된장찌개, 갈비탕.

For times of day, attach 에 (at): 아침에, 점심에, 저녁에, 밤에 (at night). 오전 = AM, 오후 = PM.

## Common Mistakes

- Saying 형 as a female — say 오빠. Korean kinship is gendered from the speaker's side.
- Confusing 밥 (rice / meal) with 빵 (bread) — different first consonant (ㅂ vs ㅃ).
- Treating 찌개 and 국 as the same — 찌개 is thicker and stew-like, served in a hot pot; 국 is brothier and served in an individual bowl.
- Using 우리 어머니 in formal contexts when you should say 저희 어머니.

## Try It Yourself

1. Introduce your family in 4 sentences using 형/오빠/누나/언니/동생.
2. Describe what you eat at each meal of the day.
3. Translate: "My grandfather likes kimchi stew."
4. Order at a restaurant: "One bibimbap and two kimbap, please." (use the right counter)

## Next Steps

Daily life covered, we extend into the public domain — school, work, and travel — where you'll meet most of your real-world Korean.

# School, Work & Travel

Vocabulary for classrooms, offices, transportation, and asking for directions. These are the words that fill subway announcements, café menus, and conversations with coworkers in Seoul, Busan, or any Korean-speaking environment.

## Core Vocabulary

| Hangul | Romanization | English |

| 학교 | hakgyo | school |
| 대학교 | daehakgyo | university |
| 학생 | haksaeng | student |

| 교실 | gyosil | classroom |
| 도서관 | doseogwan | library |
| 책 | chaek | book |
| 공책 | gongchaek | notebook |
| 시험 | siheom | exam |
| 숙제 | sukje | homework |
| 회사 | hoesa | company |
| 사무실 | samusil | office |
| 일 | il | work / a thing / day |
| 직장 | jikjang | workplace |
| 사장님 | sajangnim | boss / president |
| 동료 | dongnyo | coworker |
| 회의 | hoeui | meeting |
| 월급 | wolgeup | salary |
| 지하철 | jihacheol | subway |
| 버스 | beoseu | bus |
| 택시 | taeksi | taxi |
| 기차 | gicha | train |
| 비행기 | bihaenggi | airplane |
| 역 | yeok | station |
| 공항 | gonghang | airport |
| 표 | pyo | ticket |
| 길 | gil | road / way |
| 오른쪽 / 왼쪽 | oreunjjok / oenjjok | right / left |
| 직진 | jikjin | straight ahead |
| 어디 | eodi | where |

## Example Sentences

- **저는 대학교에서 한국어를 공부해요.** (Jeoneun daehakgyoeseo hangugeoreul gongbuhaeyo.) — I study Korean at university.
- **내일 회의가 있어요.** (Naeil hoeuiga isseoyo.) — There's a meeting tomorrow.
- **지하철역이 어디예요?** (Jihacheolyeogi eodiyeyo?) — Where is the subway station?
- **공항까지 택시로 가요.** (Gonghangkkaji taeksiro gayo.) — I'm going to the airport by taxi.
- **여기서 오른쪽으로 가세요.** (Yeogiseo oreunjjogeuro gaseyo.) — Go right from here.
- **표 두 장 주세요.** (Pyo du jang juseyo.) — Two tickets, please.

## Grammar / Script Notes

**(으)로** marks "by means of" or "toward": 버스로 (by bus), 학교로 (toward school). Use 로 after vowels and ㄹ; 으로 after other consonants. 지하철로, 택시로, but 손으로 ("by hand").

**까지** marks the endpoint or limit: 서울에서 부산까지 (from Seoul to Busan). Pair it with 부터 (starting from) or 에서 (from/at) for "from X to Y": 9시부터 5시까지 (from 9 to 5).

For directions, the verbs 가다 (go) and 오다 (come) take 에 with the destination, but the *route* takes 으로/로: 학교에 버스로 가요 ("I go to school by bus"). 직진하다 (go straight), 돌다 (turn) — 오른쪽으로 도세요 (turn right).

Korean loves Sino-Korean compounds for institutions: 대(big)+학교(school) = 대학교 (university); 회(meet)+사(company) = 회사 (company); 사(business)+무(affair)+실(room) = 사무실 (office). Decoding the Hanja roots helps you guess vocabulary.

## Common Mistakes

- Asking *어디 있어요? without a particle on the noun: it should be 지하철역이 어디 있어요? or simply 지하철역이 어디예요?
- Confusing 학교 (school in general / K-12) with 대학교 (university) — students often shorten 대학교 to 대학.
- Using 에 instead of 으로/로 for transport: *버스에 가요 means "I go to the bus"; 버스로 가요 means "I go by bus".
- Forgetting that 일 has multiple meanings: "work", "thing/matter", "day" (as in 월요일 Monday). Context disambiguates.

## Try It Yourself

1. Tell someone your major and where you study using -에서 and 공부하다.
2. Give directions from your home to the nearest subway station in 3 sentences.
3. Translate: "I take the bus to work every morning."
4. Ask three travel questions: "Where is the airport? How much is the ticket? When does the train leave?"

## Next Steps

You now have vocabulary for daily, family, food, and public life. Time to put it to use in real conversation — starting with greetings and self-introductions in the next unit.

# Greetings & Self-Introduction

Korean greetings reflect a deeply hierarchical society. The same "hello" changes form based on the listener's age, status, and your relationship — choose well, because using 안녕 with a stranger or 안녕하십니까 with a close friend both feel jarring.

## Core Vocabulary

| Hangul | Romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| 안녕하세요 | annyeonghaseyo | hello (polite) |
| 안녕하십니까 | annyeonghasimnikka | hello (formal, very polite) |
| 안녕 | annyeong | hi / bye (casual) |
| 반갑습니다 | bangapseumnida | nice to meet you (formal) |
| 반가워요 | bangawoyo | nice to meet you (polite) |
| 처음 뵙겠습니다 | cheoeum boepgesseumnida | how do you do (first meeting) |
| 제 이름은 ... 입니다 | je ireumeun ... imnida | my name is ... |
| 저는 ... 입니다 | jeoneun ... imnida | I am ... |
| 이름이 뭐예요? | ireumi mwoyeyo? | what is your name? |
| 어디에서 오셨어요? | eodieseo osyeosseoyo? | where are you from? |
| 저는 미국에서 왔어요 | jeoneun migugeseo wasseoyo | I'm from the US |
| 만나서 반갑습니다 | mannaseo bangapseumnida | nice to meet you |
| 잘 부탁드립니다 | jal butakdeurimnida | I look forward to working with you |
| 안녕히 가세요 | annyeonghi gaseyo | goodbye (to one leaving) |
| 안녕히 계세요 | annyeonghi gyeseyo | goodbye (to one staying) |
| 또 봐요 | tto bwayo | see you again |
| 감사합니다 | gamsahamnida | thank you (formal) |
| 고맙습니다 | gomapseumnida | thank you (polite) |
| 죄송합니다 | joesonghamnida | I'm sorry (formal) |
| 네 / 아니요 | ne / aniyo | yes / no |

## Example Sentences

- **안녕하세요, 저는 사라입니다.** (annyeonghaseyo, jeoneun saraimnida) — Hello, I am Sarah.
- **처음 뵙겠습니다. 잘 부탁드립니다.** (cheoeum boepgesseumnida. jal butakdeurimnida) — How do you do. I look forward to our acquaintance.
- **저는 캐나다에서 왔어요.** (jeoneun kaenadaeseo wasseoyo) — I came from Canada.
- **만나서 정말 반가워요.** (mannaseo jeongmal bangawoyo) — Really nice to meet you.
- **이름이 어떻게 되세요?** (ireumi eotteoke doeseyo?) — What is your name? (very polite)
- **안녕히 가세요!** (annyeonghi gaseyo!) — Goodbye! (said to someone leaving)

## Grammar / Script Notes

The two goodbyes — 안녕히 가세요 (go in peace) and 안녕히 계세요 (stay in peace) — are not interchangeable. The leaver says 계세요 to the one staying; the stayer says 가세요 to the one leaving. If you both leave, both say 가세요.

이름이 뭐예요? is the casual-polite form. The honorific 성함이 어떻게 되세요? (seonghami eotteoke doeseyo?) literally "how does your honorable name come to be?" is the right question for an older stranger or a business setting. Asking 이름이 뭐예요? to a 60-year-old halmeoni feels rude.

The 잘 부탁드립니다 phrase has no English equivalent — it's a humble plea for the listener to "take care of you" in the upcoming relationship. Always say it after introducing yourself in a school, workplace, or formal context.

## Common Mistakes

- Using 안녕 with anyone older or a stranger — always default to 안녕하세요.
- Saying 안녕히 가세요 when you are the one leaving — you say 계세요 to the one staying.
- Pronouncing 감사합니다 as "kam-sa-ham-ni-da" with hard k — it's a soft, unaspirated ㄱ.

## Try It Yourself

1. Introduce yourself in 4 sentences: 안녕하세요, name, where you're from, 잘 부탁드립니다.
2. Roleplay leaving a friend's house — who says 가세요 vs 계세요?
3. Greet a teacher (안녕하십니까) and a child (안녕) — feel the register difference.
4. Translate: "Nice to meet you. My name is Alex and I'm from Australia."

## Next Steps

Next up: shopping and restaurants — where you'll deploy numbers, polite requests, and the verb 주세요 constantly.

# Shopping & Restaurants

Korean service interactions run on the verb 주세요 (juseyo, "please give"). Whether you're ordering 김치찌개 or buying a SIM card, attaching 주세요 to a noun gets you 80% of the way there.

## Core Vocabulary

|--------|--------------|---------|

| 시장 | sijang | market |
| 백화점 | baekhwajeom | department store |
| 식당 | sikdang | restaurant |
| 메뉴 | menyu | menu |
| 주문하다 | jumunhada | to order |
| 계산하다 | gyesanhada | to pay / settle the bill |
| 얼마예요? | eolmayeyo? | how much is it? |
| 비싸요 | bissayo | it's expensive |
| 싸요 | ssayo | it's cheap |
| 깎아 주세요 | kkakka juseyo | please give a discount |
| 이거 주세요 | igeo juseyo | I'll have this one (please) |
| 물 좀 주세요 | mul jom juseyo | please give me water |
| 여기요 / 저기요 | yeogiyo / jeogiyo | excuse me (calling staff) |
| 맛있어요 | masisseoyo | it's delicious |
| 매워요 | maewoyo | it's spicy |
| 영수증 | yeongsujeung | receipt |
| 카드로 할게요 | kadeuro halgeyo | I'll pay by card |
| 현금 | hyeongeum | cash |
| 포장해 주세요 | pojanghae juseyo | please pack it to go |
| 더 주세요 | deo juseyo | please give me more |
| 잘 먹겠습니다 | jal meokgesseumnida | I will eat well (pre-meal) |
| 잘 먹었습니다 | jal meogeosseumnida | I ate well (post-meal) |

## Example Sentences

- **이거 얼마예요?** (igeo eolmayeyo?) — How much is this?
- **김치찌개 하나 주세요.** (gimchijjigae hana juseyo) — One kimchi stew, please.
- **너무 비싸요. 좀 깎아 주세요.** (neomu bissayo. jom kkakka juseyo) — Too expensive. Please discount a little.
- **저기요, 물 좀 더 주세요.** (jeogiyo, mul jom deo juseyo) — Excuse me, more water please.
- **카드로 계산할게요.** (kadeuro gyesanhalgeyo) — I'll pay by card.
- **잘 먹었습니다!** (jal meogeosseumnida) — Thanks for the meal! (said when leaving)

## Grammar / Script Notes

주세요 attaches to either a noun (이거 주세요 — give me this) or the **-아/어 주세요** form of a verb (도와주세요 — please help me; 깎아 주세요 — please discount). The verb form is a polite request: "do X for me."

Numbers in restaurants use **native Korean** with counters: 하나 (one), 둘 (two), 셋 (three) — but before a counter they shorten: 한 개 (one item), 두 명 (two people), 세 그릇 (three bowls). Sino-Korean numbers (일, 이, 삼) are for prices, dates, and phone numbers: 만 원 (10,000 won), not *한만 원*.

여기요 and 저기요 both work to call a server, but 저기요 (literally "over there") is slightly softer because it doesn't presume the server is right next to you. In a quiet restaurant, 사장님 (sajangnim, "boss") or 이모 (imo, "auntie") works in casual eateries.

## Common Mistakes

- Saying 비싸 instead of 비싸요 to a vendor — drop the -요 only with close friends.
- Using 일, 이, 삼 to count people: it's 한 명, 두 명, 세 명, never *일 명*.
- Forgetting 잘 먹겠습니다 before eating — it's expected at home meals and in many restaurants when food arrives.

## Try It Yourself

1. Order three dishes at a Korean restaurant using "X 하나 주세요."
2. Bargain in a market: ask the price, say it's expensive, ask for a discount.
3. Practice 잘 먹겠습니다 / 잘 먹었습니다 with the right timing.
4. Translate: "Excuse me, the bibimbap is too spicy. Please give me water."

## Next Steps

Next: making plans and phone calls — where you'll learn time expressions, scheduling verbs, and Korean phone etiquette.

# Making Plans & Phone Conversations

Calling and texting in Korean uses a distinct register — the answerer leads with 여보세요, calendars run on Sino-Korean numerals, and refusals are softened by phrases like 좀 어려울 것 같아요 (it might be a bit difficult).

## Core Vocabulary

| 여보세요 | yeoboseyo | hello (on phone) |
| 전화하다 | jeonhwahada | to call |

| 문자 | munja | text message |
| 약속 | yaksok | appointment / promise |
| 약속을 잡다 | yaksogeul japda | to make an appointment |
| 만나다 | mannada | to meet |
| 시간이 있어요? | sigani isseoyo? | do you have time? |
| 언제 | eonje | when |
| 어디서 | eodiseo | where |
| 몇 시에 | myeot sie | at what time |
| 내일 | naeil | tomorrow |
| 모레 | more | the day after tomorrow |
| 주말 | jumal | weekend |
| 다음 주 | daeum ju | next week |
| 같이 갈래요? | gachi gallaeyo? | want to go together? |

| 미안해요, 안 돼요 | mianhaeyo, an dwaeyo | sorry, I can't |
| 나중에 다시 | najunge dasi | again later |
| 끊을게요 | kkeuneulgeyo | I'll hang up |
| 잠시만요 | jamsimanyo | just a moment |
| 누구세요? | nuguseyo? | who is this? |

## Example Sentences

- **여보세요, 민지 씨 계세요?** (yeoboseyo, minji ssi gyeseyo?) — Hello, is Minji there?
- **내일 저녁에 시간 있어요?** (naeil jeonyeoge sigan isseoyo?) — Do you have time tomorrow evening?
- **토요일 7시에 강남역에서 만나요.** (toyoil ilgop sie gangnamyeogeseo mannayo) — Let's meet at Gangnam Station at 7 on Saturday.
- **죄송하지만 주말에는 좀 어려울 것 같아요.** (joesonghajiman jumareneun jom eoryeoul geot gatayo) — Sorry, the weekend might be a little difficult.
- **알겠어요. 그럼 다음 주에 봐요.** (algesseoyo. geureom daeum jue bwayo) — Got it. Then see you next week.
- **잠시만요, 메모 좀 할게요.** (jamsimanyo, memo jom halgeyo) — One moment, let me take a note.

## Grammar / Script Notes

Time uses **native Korean for hours** and **Sino-Korean for minutes**: 7시 30분 = 일곱 시 삼십 분 (ilgop si samsip bun). Saying *칠 시 삼십 분* is a classic learner mistake — hours are 한 시, 두 시, 세 시 ... 열두 시.

Refusals are softened in Korean. Instead of 안 가요 (I'm not going), Koreans say 좀 어려울 것 같아요 (it seems a bit difficult) or 다음에 갈게요 (I'll go next time). Direct "no" can sound cold; cushion it with 죄송하지만 (sorry, but).

Phone openers: the caller usually says 여보세요, then identifies — 저는 ... 인데요 (I am ..., and ...). The connective -ㄴ데요 leaves the sentence open, inviting the listener to respond. Closing the call: 그럼 끊을게요 (well, I'll hang up) is normal, but seniors often hear 들어가세요 (please go in) instead.

## Common Mistakes

- Mixing number systems: *칠 시* for 7 o'clock — it's 일곱 시.
- Saying *아니요* flatly to refuse a meeting — soften with 죄송한데요 first.
- Using 안녕하세요 to open a phone call — phone openers are 여보세요.

## Try It Yourself

1. Call a friend in Korean: greet, ask if they're free Saturday at 6, suggest a place.
2. Politely refuse two invitations using different soft-refusal phrases.
3. Practice telling time: 3:15, 6:45, 11:30 — mixing native and Sino-Korean.
4. Translate: "Hello? Is this Minho? It's Sara. Are you free tomorrow morning?"

# Reading Hangul Texts

Once you can decode syllable blocks, the next leap is **fluent reading** — parsing particles, recognizing common verb endings at a glance, and predicting unfamiliar words from context.

## Core Vocabulary

| Hangul | Romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| 읽다 | ikda | to read |
| 보다 | boda | to look / read (casual) |
| 글 | geul | writing / text |
| 책 | chaek | book |
| 신문 | sinmun | newspaper |
| 잡지 | japji | magazine |
| 간판 | ganpan | sign / signboard |
| 메뉴판 | menyupan | menu board |
| 광고 | gwanggo | advertisement |
| 제목 | jemok | title |
| 문장 | munjang | sentence |
| 단락 | dallak | paragraph |
| 단어 | daneo | word |
| 뜻 | tteut | meaning |
| 사전 | sajeon | dictionary |
| 한자 | hanja | Chinese character |
| 받침 | batchim | final consonant |
| 띄어쓰기 | ttuieosseugi | spacing |
| 맞춤법 | matchumbeop | spelling / orthography |
| 이해하다 | ihaehada | to understand |
| 외우다 | oeuda | to memorize |

## Example Sentences

- **이 책 제목이 뭐예요?** (i chaek jemogi mwoyeyo?) — What's the title of this book?
- **간판에 뭐라고 쓰여 있어요?** (ganpane mworago sseuyeo isseoyo?) — What does the sign say?
- **이 단어의 뜻을 모르겠어요.** (i daneoui tteuseul moreugesseoyo) — I don't know the meaning of this word.
- **사전에서 찾아볼게요.** (sajeoneseo chajabolgeyo) — I'll look it up in the dictionary.
- **천천히 읽으면 이해할 수 있어요.** (cheoncheonhi ilgeumyeon ihaehal su isseoyo) — If you read slowly, you can understand.
- **이 문장이 너무 어려워요.** (i munjangi neomu eoryeowoyo) — This sentence is too difficult.

## Grammar / Script Notes

Korean **spacing** (띄어쓰기) is meaning-bearing. 아버지가방에들어가신다 reads as either 아버지가 방에 들어가신다 (Father enters the room) or 아버지 가방에 들어가신다 (Father enters the bag). Always space after particles and between content words.

Read by **syllable block, not letter**. 학교 is two units (학 + 교 = "school"), not five letters. With practice, multi-block words become single visual chunks: 한국어, 안녕하세요, 감사합니다.

Common particles to spot quickly: **-은/는** (topic), **-이/가** (subject), **-을/를** (object), **-에/에서** (location), **-와/과/하고** (and/with), **-도** (also), **-만** (only), **-부터/까지** (from/to). They cling to the noun's right, so finding them tells you the noun's role in the sentence.

## Common Mistakes

- Reading letter-by-letter instead of by syllable block — slows reading dramatically.
- Ignoring 받침 (final consonants) — 갈 vs 가 are different verbs.
- Confusing similar-shaped letters: ㅁ vs ㅇ, ㄹ vs ㄴ in fast handwriting.

## Try It Yourself

1. Read a Korean menu and identify three dishes with their prices.
2. Take a photo of a Korean street sign and decode it without translation.
3. Pick a children's book — read aloud at 60% speed, syllable by syllable.
4. Find five sentences in a K-drama subtitle and circle every particle.

## Next Steps

Next we move from reading to writing — constructing sentences and short paragraphs of your own.

# Writing Sentences & Paragraphs

Korean writing follows **SOV order** (Subject-Object-Verb) and demands attention to particles, verb endings, and politeness register. A grammatically correct sentence in 합니다체 (formal) and 해요체 (polite) often differs only in the final ending.

## Core Vocabulary

| Hangul | Romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| 쓰다 | sseuda | to write |
| 적다 | jeokda | to jot down |
| 짓다 | jitda | to compose |
| 일기 | ilgi | diary |
| 편지 | pyeonji | letter |
| 이메일 | imeil | email |
| 문법 | munbeop | grammar |
| 주어 | jueo | subject |
| 목적어 | mokjeogeo | object |
| 서술어 | seosureo | predicate |
| 조사 | josa | particle |
| 어미 | eomi | verb ending |
| 시제 | sije | tense |
| 존댓말 | jondaetmal | honorific speech |
| 반말 | banmal | casual speech |
| 머리말 | meorimal | introduction |
| 본문 | bonmun | main body |
| 결론 | gyeollon | conclusion |
| 고치다 | gochida | to correct |
| 다시 쓰다 | dasi sseuda | to rewrite |

## Example Sentences

- **저는 매일 일기를 써요.** (jeoneun maeil ilgireul sseoyo) — I write a diary every day.
- **선생님께 편지를 썼어요.** (seonsaengnimkke pyeonjireul sseosseoyo) — I wrote a letter to the teacher.
- **이 문장은 문법이 틀렸어요.** (i munjangeun munbeobi teullyeosseoyo) — This sentence is grammatically wrong.
- **주어와 서술어가 맞지 않아요.** (jueowa seosureoga matji anayo) — The subject and predicate don't agree.
- **다시 한번 써 보세요.** (dasi hanbeon sseo boseyo) — Try writing it once more.
- **존댓말로 바꿔 주세요.** (jondaetmallo bakkwo juseyo) — Please change it to honorific speech.

## Grammar / Script Notes

A canonical Korean sentence: **Subject + (Object) + Verb**.
- 저는 한국어를 공부해요. (jeoneun hangugeoreul gongbuhaeyo) — I study Korean.
- 친구가 책을 읽어요. (chinguga chaegeul ilgeoyo) — My friend reads a book.

The topic particle **은/는** vs the subject particle **이/가** is subtle: 은/는 introduces the topic ("as for X"), while 이/가 marks new or contrastive subjects. In your first paragraph sentence, prefer 은/는; for follow-ups about a new subject, switch to 이/가.

Verb endings carry tense AND register simultaneously:
- Present polite: 가요 (gayo)
- Past polite: 갔어요 (gasseoyo)
- Future polite: 갈 거예요 (gal geoyeyo)
- Formal: 갑니다 / 갔습니다 / 갈 것입니다.

When writing, pick one register and stay there. Mixing 합니다체 and 해요체 mid-paragraph reads as inconsistent.

## Common Mistakes

- Putting the verb in the middle: *저는 공부해요 한국어를* — verb must come last.
- Using 은/는 every time — overuse blurs the contrast it's meant to show.
- Mixing -요 and -ㅂ니다 endings in one paragraph.

## Try It Yourself

1. Write a 5-sentence diary entry about today: where you went, what you ate, who you met.
2. Translate into Korean: "Yesterday I read a book. The book was interesting. I want to read it again tomorrow."
3. Take a paragraph in 해요체 and rewrite in 합니다체.
4. Email a Korean teacher introducing yourself in 6 sentences, using full honorifics.

## Next Steps

Next we open the door to **Hanja** — the Chinese characters lurking inside half of Korean vocabulary.

# Hanja Basics & Mixed Script

Roughly **60–70% of Korean vocabulary** is Sino-Korean, originally written in Chinese characters (한자, Hanja). Modern Korean uses Hangul almost exclusively, but Hanja appears in newspapers, legal texts, names, and disambiguating homophones.

## Core Vocabulary

| Hanja | Hangul | Romanization | English |
|-------|--------|--------------|---------|
| 人 | 인 | in | person |
| 大 | 대 | dae | big |
| 小 | 소 | so | small |
| 水 | 수 | su | water |
| 山 | 산 | san | mountain |
| 日 | 일 | il | day / sun |
| 月 | 월 | wol | month / moon |
| 年 | 년 | nyeon | year |
| 學 | 학 | hak | study |
| 校 | 교 | gyo | school |
| 國 | 국 | guk | country |
| 韓 | 한 | han | Korea |
| 中 | 중 | jung | middle / China |
| 美 | 미 | mi | beautiful / America |
| 父 | 부 | bu | father |
| 母 | 모 | mo | mother |
| 男 | 남 | nam | male / south |
| 女 | 녀 | nyeo | female |
| 上 | 상 | sang | above |
| 下 | 하 | ha | below |
| 東西南北 | 동서남북 | dongseonambuk | east-west-south-north |

## Example Words & Sentences

- **學校 → 학교** (hakgyo) — school (study + school)
- **大學 → 대학** (daehak) — university (big + study)
- **韓國人 → 한국인** (hangugin) — Korean person
- **美國 → 미국** (miguk) — America
- **新聞에 큰 사건이 났어요.** (sinmune keun sageoni nasseoyo) — A big incident appeared in the newspaper.
- **金 박사님은 大學 교수입니다.** (Kim baksanimeun daehak gyosuimnida) — Dr. Kim is a university professor. (mixed-script style)

## Grammar / Script Notes

Hanja in modern Korea appears in three places:
1. **Names** — Korean names are usually two Hanja characters: 김민수 = 金 (gold) + 民 (people) + 秀 (excellent).
2. **Newspapers** — headlines may add Hanja in parentheses for clarity: 정상 (頂上) 회담.
3. **Legal & academic texts** — to disambiguate homophones: 의사 (醫師, doctor) vs 의사 (意思, intention).

Each Hanja character has one main Korean reading (음, eum) and a meaning gloss (훈, hun). The character 山 is read 산 (san) and means 메 (me, "mountain"). When children learn Hanja, they recite "메 산" (mountain — san).

Hanja words follow Chinese morphology: **modifier + head**. 大學 = "big study" = university; 學生 = "study person" = student; 國民 = "country people" = citizen. Once you spot the building blocks, hundreds of new words unlock.

## Common Mistakes

- Trying to learn Hanja before solid Hangul reading — it adds load too early.
- Assuming every Korean word has Hanja — pure Korean (고유어) words like 하늘 (sky), 바다 (sea), 사랑 (love) have no Hanja origin.
- Reading 中 as Chinese 'zhōng' — the Korean reading is 중 (jung).

## Try It Yourself

1. Write your own Korean name in Hanja (ask a Korean speaker for help if needed).
2. Find five university or company names with 大學 / 大 and decode each character.
3. Pick a Korean newspaper headline with mixed script — identify each Hanja's hangul reading.
4. Memorize the 20 characters in the table above. Quiz: meaning + reading for each.

## Next Steps

Next we shift from script to society — exploring Korean social etiquette, hierarchy, and unwritten rules.

# Korean Social Etiquette

Korean society runs on **나이 (nai, age)** and **지위 (jiwi, status)**. Within minutes of meeting, Koreans often exchange ages and titles — not from rudeness, but to know which speech level and pronouns to use. Misreading the hierarchy is the single biggest source of friction for foreigners.

## Core Vocabulary

| Hangul | Romanization | English |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| 예의 | yeui | etiquette / manners |
| 예의 바르다 | yeui bareuda | to be well-mannered |
| 어른 | eoreun | adult / elder |
| 윗사람 | witsaram | superior / elder |
| 아랫사람 | araetsaram | junior / subordinate |
| 선배 | seonbae | senior (school/work) |
| 후배 | hubae | junior (school/work) |
| 형 / 오빠 | hyeong / oppa | older brother (m / f speaker) |
| 누나 / 언니 | nuna / eonni | older sister (m / f speaker) |
| 인사하다 | insahada | to greet / bow |
| 절하다 | jeolhada | to do a deep bow |
| 고개를 숙이다 | gogaereul sugida | to lower one's head |
| 두 손으로 | du soneuro | with two hands |
| 나이 | nai | age |
| 빠른 ... 년생 | ppareun ... nyeonsaeng | early-year-born (school year boundary) |
| 존댓말 | jondaetmal | polite/formal speech |
| 반말 | banmal | casual speech |
| 말 놓다 | mal nota | to drop into casual speech |
| 선물 | seonmul | gift |
| 술자리 | suljari | drinking gathering |
| 더치페이 | deochipei | dutch pay (split bill) |

## Example Sentences

- **나이가 어떻게 되세요?** (naiga eotteoke doeseyo?) — May I ask your age? (politely)
- **저보다 한 살 위시네요.** (jeoboda han sal wisineyo) — You're one year older than me.
- **그럼 형이라고 부를게요.** (geureom hyeongirago bureulgeyo) — Then I'll call you 'older brother'.
- **선배님께 두 손으로 드리세요.** (seonbaenimkke du soneuro deuriseyo) — Hand it to your senior with two hands.
- **저희 말 놓을까요?** (jeohui mal noeulkkayo?) — Shall we drop into casual speech?
- **오늘은 제가 살게요.** (oneureun jega salgeyo) — Today I'll treat (pay).

## Cultural Notes

**Bowing**: a 15° head-and-shoulders dip is the everyday bow used in 안녕하세요. A 30° bow is for first-meet formality or expressing thanks. The full 큰절 (kneeling bow) is reserved for elders on holidays (Seollal) or weddings.

**Two hands**: when receiving or giving anything to someone older — money, business cards, a glass — use both hands. The free hand can support the giving wrist if the object is small. One-handing a senior's business card is genuinely rude.

**Age and titles**: once age is established, the older person becomes 형/오빠/누나/언니 (for friends) or 선배 (for school/work). Korean classmates born in early Jan/Feb (빠른 년생) traditionally counted with the prior school year — this convention is fading post-2010.

**Drinking culture (술자리)**: pour drinks for others, never your own. Turn your face slightly away when drinking in front of an elder. Receive your glass with two hands. Offer to top up your senior's glass when it's half empty.

## Common Mistakes

- Calling an older Korean by name without 씨 / 님 / 형 / 누나 — feels disrespectful.
- Pouring your own drink in a group setting — let someone else pour.
- Refusing a senior's offer to pay — let them pay; you treat next time.

## Try It Yourself

1. Practice the 15° bow in front of a mirror — back straight, eyes slightly down.
2. Roleplay a meeting: exchange names, ages, agree on whether to use 존댓말 or 반말.
3. Receive a "business card" with two hands and a small bow.
4. Translate: "May I ask your age? Then I'll call you older sister."

| 성묘 | seongmyo | visiting ancestral graves |
| 송편 | songpyeon | half-moon rice cake (Chuseok) |

| 무속 | musok | shamanism |

- **설날 아침에 떡국을 먹어요.** (seollal achime tteokgugeul meogeoyo) — On Seollal morning we eat tteokguk.
- **할머니께 세배를 드렸어요.** (halmeonikke sebaereul deuryeosseoyo) — I made a New Year bow to grandma.
- **아이들이 세뱃돈을 받았어요.** (aideuri sebaetdoneul badasseoyo) — The children received New Year money.

Korean (한국어) is spoken by over 77 million people. It uses Hangul, a scientifically designed alphabet created by King Sejong the Great in 1443. Korean is an SOV language with complex honorific systems.

**Reported Speech & Quoting** is a crucial component of learning Korean. Indirect speech patterns: -다고 하다, -냐고 하다, -라고 하다

## Why Learn Reported Speech & Quoting?

Mastering reported speech & quoting will enable you to:
- Communicate more naturally and accurately in Korean
- Understand native speakers in real conversations
- Read authentic Korean texts with comprehension
- Express yourself with confidence in various social situations
- Build a strong foundation for advanced language study

## Core Content

### Key Points
1. Reported Speech & Quoting follows specific patterns in Korean that differ from English
2. Regular practice with authentic materials accelerates learning
3. Understanding the cultural context enhances communication
4. Building connections between new and known concepts aids retention
5. Active production (speaking and writing) solidifies passive knowledge (listening and reading)

### Essential Vocabulary for Reported Speech & Quoting
Learning vocabulary in context is more effective than memorizing word lists. Here are strategies specific to reported speech & quoting:
- Create flashcards with example sentences, not just translations
- Group words by theme, situation, or grammatical category
- Practice pronunciation of each new word immediately
- Use new vocabulary in writing within 24 hours of learning it
- Review vocabulary using spaced repetition (TopicTree has this built in!)

### Grammar Points Related to Reported Speech & Quoting
Grammar and vocabulary work together. As you study reported speech & quoting, pay attention to:
- How words change form in different contexts
- Word order rules specific to this topic
- Agreement patterns (gender, number, case, etc.)
- Common exceptions and irregular forms
- How Korean grammar compares to English grammar for this topic


## Historical Background

Understanding the history of Korean helps contextualize its modern form. The language has evolved over centuries, influenced by trade, colonization, religion, and cultural exchange. Key historical periods shaped the vocabulary, grammar, and writing system used today. Learning this history deepens your appreciation and helps you understand why certain rules exist.

## Phonology Deep Dive

The sound system of Korean has unique features that English speakers must master. Pay careful attention to sounds that don't exist in English. Practice minimal pairs (words that differ by only one sound) to train your ear. Record yourself and compare with native speakers. Tongue position, lip rounding, and airflow all matter for accurate pronunciation.

## Writing System Details

The Korean writing system has its own logic and beauty. Practice writing by hand — this builds muscle memory and helps with recognition. Start with basic characters/letters and progress to complex combinations. Pay attention to stroke order where applicable, as it affects the appearance and readability of your writing.

## Grammar in Depth

Grammar is the skeleton of any language. In Korean, pay special attention to word order, agreement rules, and how meaning changes with different structures. Don't try to memorize every rule — instead, learn patterns through example sentences. Grammar becomes intuitive with enough exposure and practice.

## Vocabulary Strategies

Building vocabulary efficiently requires strategy. Use the following techniques: (1) Learn words in context, not isolation. (2) Group related words together (semantic fields). (3) Use mnemonics and associations. (4) Review with spaced repetition. (5) Learn high-frequency words first — the 1000 most common words cover about 85% of everyday speech.

## Listening Comprehension

Developing listening skills requires regular exposure to authentic Korean audio. Start with slow, clear speech (podcasts for learners) and gradually increase difficulty to native-speed content. Watch movies, TV shows, and YouTube videos. Use subtitles initially, then wean off them. Focus on understanding the gist before worrying about every word.

## Speaking Practice

Speaking is often the most challenging skill because it requires real-time production. Start by shadowing (repeating after audio), then practice scripted dialogues, then move to free conversation. Don't worry about perfection — fluency comes before accuracy. Find language exchange partners through apps like Tandem or HelloTalk.

## Reading Skills

Reading in Korean builds vocabulary passively and reinforces grammar patterns. Start with children's books, graded readers, or news in simplified language. Use the extensive reading approach: read material slightly below your level for pleasure, without looking up every word. This builds reading speed and natural language feel.

## Common Errors Analysis

English speakers make predictable errors when learning Korean. Common mistakes include: applying English word order, mispronouncing sounds unique to Korean, forgetting agreement rules, and using false cognates (words that look similar but mean different things). Awareness of these patterns helps you avoid them.

## Real-World Application

Language learning becomes meaningful when applied to real situations. Try: ordering food at a Korean restaurant, writing a letter/email, following a recipe, reading product labels, navigating a website, or having a conversation with a native speaker. Each real-world interaction reinforces what you've learned and reveals gaps in your knowledge.

## Test Preparation

If you're preparing for a Korean proficiency test, focus on: timed reading practice, listening to recorded passages and answering questions, writing structured essays, and speaking for extended periods on given topics. Familiarize yourself with the test format and practice under timed conditions.

## Media Recommendations

Immerse yourself in Korean through media: follow social media accounts, listen to music (look up lyrics), watch popular TV series with subtitles, read blogs and news sites, subscribe to YouTube channels for learners. This makes learning enjoyable and sustainable long-term.

### Beginner Level
1. Identify key concepts from this lesson in a simple text
2. Translate 5 basic sentences using concepts from this topic
3. Write a short paragraph (3-4 sentences) using new vocabulary
4. Listen to a beginner audio clip and identify words you know
5. Practice pronunciation by recording yourself and comparing

### Intermediate Level
1. Read a short article and summarize the main points
2. Write a dialogue using the grammar patterns from this lesson
3. Listen to a podcast episode and take notes in Korean
4. Have a 5-minute conversation using these concepts
5. Translate a paragraph from English maintaining natural Korean structure

### Advanced Level
1. Write an essay (200+ words) incorporating all concepts from this lesson
2. Debate a topic using formal register and advanced vocabulary
3. Translate a complex text preserving nuance and tone
4. Give a 3-minute presentation on a topic related to this lesson
5. Analyze authentic Korean media for examples of these concepts

## Cultural Integration

Language and culture are inseparable. As you study reported speech & quoting, consider:
- How do native speakers use these concepts in daily life?
- What cultural values are reflected in the language choices?
- How does context (formal vs informal, written vs spoken) affect usage?
- What regional variations exist for these concepts?
- How has globalization influenced modern usage?

Rate yourself on each skill (1-5):
- [ ] I can recognize these concepts when reading
- [ ] I can understand these concepts when listening
- [ ] I can produce these concepts when writing
- [ ] I can use these concepts when speaking
- [ ] I understand the cultural context
- [ ] I can explain these concepts to another learner

Comparing Korean with English and other languages helps identify transfer opportunities and interference patterns. Where languages share features, learning is accelerated through positive transfer. Where they differ, learners must be extra vigilant.

### Similarities with English
Some Korean concepts parallel English structures, which can accelerate learning. Identify these similarities and use them as anchors for new knowledge. However, be cautious of false friends (words that look or sound similar but have different meanings).

### Key Differences from English
Understanding fundamental differences prevents common errors. These differences include word order, morphological complexity, phonological inventory, writing system, and pragmatic conventions. Explicit awareness of these differences is the first step to mastering them.

### Connection to Other Languages
Korean shares features with related languages. Understanding these connections can help if you already speak another language in the same family. Cross-linguistic awareness is a powerful tool for polyglots.

### Scenario 1: At the Airport
Imagine you are arriving in a Korean-speaking country. Practice vocabulary and phrases for: checking in, going through customs, asking for directions, finding transportation, and checking into a hotel.

### Scenario 2: At a Restaurant
Practice ordering food, asking about ingredients, making special requests, complimenting the chef, paying the bill, and leaving a tip (where culturally appropriate).

### Scenario 3: Shopping
Practice asking about prices, sizes, colors, trying things on, bargaining (where appropriate), paying, and returning items.

### Scenario 4: Medical Emergency
Practice describing symptoms, understanding a doctor's questions, explaining allergies and medications, and following medical instructions. This is critical for travelers.

### Scenario 5: Making Friends
Practice introducing yourself, asking about hobbies and interests, making plans, exchanging contact information, and maintaining friendships.

### Scenario 6: At Work/School
Practice professional greetings, asking questions, presenting ideas, scheduling meetings, and writing professional emails or messages.

### Top 100 Most Useful Words
The most frequently used words in Korean cover approximately 50 percent of all speech. Master these first:
- Personal pronouns (I, you, he/she/it, we, they)
- Basic verbs (be, have, go, come, do, make, say, know, want, can)
- Question words (who, what, where, when, why, how)
- Common nouns (person, time, day, thing, place, world)
- Adjectives (good, bad, big, small, new, old, young)
- Conjunctions (and, but, or, because, if, when)
- Prepositions/postpositions (in, on, at, to, from, with)

### Academic Vocabulary
For students and professionals: terms for education, research, presentation, analysis, argument, evidence, conclusion, methodology, and academic writing conventions.

### Emotional Vocabulary
Expressing emotions accurately shows language sophistication: happy, sad, angry, surprised, afraid, disgusted, embarrassed, proud, jealous, grateful, confused, excited, bored, anxious, relieved.

## Pronunciation Guide

### Mouth Position Diagrams (Described)
For each unique sound in Korean, the correct mouth position involves specific placement of:
- Tongue (tip, blade, body, root)
- Lips (rounded, spread, neutral)
- Jaw (open, mid, closed)
- Soft palate (raised for oral sounds, lowered for nasal)
- Vocal cords (voiced or voiceless)

### Rhythm and Intonation
Every language has its own rhythm pattern. Korean has specific stress patterns, intonation contours for questions vs statements, and rhythm characteristics (stress-timed, syllable-timed, or mora-timed) that learners must internalize.

### Connected Speech
In natural speech, words flow together and sounds change. Common processes include: assimilation (sounds becoming more similar), elision (sounds being dropped), liaison (sounds being linked), and reduction (unstressed syllables becoming shorter).

## Language Learning Science

### How Memory Works for Language
- Short-term memory holds new vocabulary for seconds
- Working memory processes grammar rules during production
- Long-term memory stores learned vocabulary and automatized grammar
- Sleep consolidates language memories (study before bed!)
- Spaced repetition optimizes the forgetting curve

### The Four Skills Framework
1. Receptive skills: Listening and Reading (input)
2. Productive skills: Speaking and Writing (output)
3. All four skills reinforce each other
4. Most learners develop receptive skills faster than productive
5. Deliberate practice in weaker skills accelerates overall progress

### Motivation and Mindset
- Set specific, measurable goals (not just 'learn Korean')
- Track your progress visually (TopicTree mastery dashboard)
- Celebrate small wins (first conversation, first book, first movie without subtitles)
- Join a community of learners for accountability
- Remember: every expert was once a beginner

Reported Speech & Quoting is an essential building block in your Korean learning journey. Consistent practice, cultural awareness, and real-world application will help you master these concepts. Use TopicTree's adaptive practice, flashcards, and spaced repetition tools to reinforce what you've learned.

**Recommended daily practice**: 15-20 minutes of focused study on this topic, plus passive exposure through Korean media throughout the day.

Tongue position, lip rounding, and airflow all matter for accurate pronunciation.

The Korean writing system has its own logic and beauty. Practice writing by hand — this builds muscle memory and helps with recognition. Start with basic characters/letters and progress to complex combinations. Pay attention to stroke order where applicable, as it affects the appearance and readability of your writing.

Grammar is the skeleton of any language. In Korean, pay special attention to word order, agreement rules, and how meaning changes with different structures. Speaking is often the most challenging skill because it requires real-time production. Start by shadowing (repeating after audio), then practice scripted dialogues, then move to free conversation. Reading in Korean builds vocabulary passively and reinforces grammar patterns. Start with children's books, graded readers, or news in simplified language. English speakers make predictable errors when learning Korean. Language learning becomes meaningful when applied to real situations.
